claim: Mothers are crucial for mammals' survival before nutritional independence.
source: Mothers are crucial for mammals' survival before nutritional independence, but many social mammals reside with their mothers long after.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus about mammalian biology.

claim: Many social mammals reside with their mothers long after nutritional independence.
source: Mothers are crucial for mammals' survival before nutritional independence, but many social mammals reside with their mothers long after.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about social mammal behavior.

claim: In some social mammal species, the social adversity caused by maternal loss later in life can dramatically reduce fitness.
source: In these species the social adversity caused by maternal loss later in life can dramatically reduce fitness.
evidence: This is supported by references to prior research on social mammals.

claim: In some human populations, negative consequences of maternal loss can be overcome by care from other group members.
source: However, in some human populations these negative consequences can be overcome by care from other group members.
evidence: This is supported by references to human population studies cited later in the manuscript.

claim: Mountain gorillas show no discernible fitness costs to maternal loss through survival.
source: We investigated the consequences of maternal loss in mountain gorillas and found no discernible fitness costs to maternal loss through survival, age at first birth, or survival of first offspring through infancy.
evidence: This is supported by the Cox-proportional hazards analysis and Bayesian survival trajectory analysis presented in the Results section.

claim: Mountain gorillas show no discernible fitness costs to maternal loss through age at first birth.
source: We investigated the consequences of maternal loss in mountain gorillas and found no discernible fitness costs to maternal loss through survival, age at first birth, or survival of first offspring through infancy.
evidence: This is supported by the generalized linear model analysis of age at first birth presented in the Results section.

claim: Mountain gorillas show no discernible fitness costs to maternal loss through survival of first offspring through infancy.
source: We investigated the consequences of maternal loss in mountain gorillas and found no discernible fitness costs to maternal loss through survival, age at first birth, or survival of first offspring through infancy.
evidence: This is supported by the binomial generalized linear model analysis of first offspring survival presented in the Results section.

claim: Relationships with other group members strengthen following maternal loss in mountain gorillas.
source: Social network analysis revealed that relationships with other group members, particularly dominant males and those close in age, strengthened following maternal loss.
evidence: This is supported by the social network analysis presented in the Results section showing increased weighted degree and eigenvector centrality.

claim: Relationships with dominant males particularly strengthen following maternal loss in mountain gorillas.
source: Social network analysis revealed that relationships with other group members, particularly dominant males and those close in age, strengthened following maternal loss.
evidence: This is supported by the GAMM analysis showing the greatest increase in relationship strength with dominant males.

claim: Relationships with those close in age particularly strengthen following maternal loss in mountain gorillas.
source: Social network analysis revealed that relationships with other group members, particularly dominant males and those close in age, strengthened following maternal loss.
evidence: This is supported by the GAMM analysis showing significant effects of age-mate status on proximity changes.

claim: In mountain gorillas, maternal loss may be buffered by relationships within cohesive social groups.
source: In contrast to most social mammals, where maternal loss causes considerable social adversity, in mountain gorillas, as in certain human populations, this may be buffered by relationships within cohesive social groups, breaking the link between maternal loss, increased social adversity, and decreased fitness.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of no fitness costs and strengthened social relationships observed in the study.

claim: Maternal loss is one of the strongest predictors of lifespan in humans and other social mammals.
source: Maternal loss, along with a number of other indicators of early-life adversity, is one of the strongest predictors of lifespan in humans and other social mammals (Snyder-Mackler et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Snyder-Mackler et al., 2020.

claim: In mammals, mothers provide nutrition, thermoregulation, and protection to young offspring.
source: In mammals, mothers are vital for the survival of young offspring, providing nutrition, thermoregulation, and protection (Clutton-Brock, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Clutton-Brock, 1991 and represents established knowledge.

claim: In some social species with slow life histories, mothers continue to provide benefits to their co-residing offspring throughout immaturity and even into adulthood.
source: In some species, particularly social species with slow life histories (Mitani et al., 2013), mothers continue to provide benefits to their co-residing offspring throughout immaturity and even into adulthood (Surbeck et al., 2019; Surbeck et al., 2011; Andres et al., 2013; Stanton et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on various species.

claim: Active support of mothers can increase the rank of their offspring.
source: The active support of mothers can increase the rank of their offspring (Strauss et al., 2020; East et al., 2009; Maestripieri and Mateo, 2009; Lea et al., 2014) and improve their integration in the group (Tung et al., 2016), both of which are linked with greater survival (Snyder-Mackler et al., 2020; Archie et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on social mammals.

claim: Active support of mothers can improve offspring integration in the group.
source: The active support of mothers can increase the rank of their offspring (Strauss et al., 2020; East et al., 2009; Maestripieri and Mateo, 2009; Lea et al., 2014) and improve their integration in the group (Tung et al., 2016), both of which are linked with greater survival (Snyder-Mackler et al., 2020; Archie et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tung et al., 2016.

claim: Offspring rank and group integration are linked with greater survival.
source: The active support of mothers can increase the rank of their offspring (Strauss et al., 2020; East et al., 2009; Maestripieri and Mateo, 2009; Lea et al., 2014) and improve their integration in the group (Tung et al., 2016), both of which are linked with greater survival (Snyder-Mackler et al., 2020; Archie et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Snyder-Mackler et al., 2020 and Archie et al., 2014.

claim: Maternal presence can influence nutrition at later stages of development by buffering against feeding competition.
source: Maternal presence can also influence nutrition at these later stages of development by buffering against feeding competition (Samuni et al., 2020), providing access to valuable ecological knowledge (Stanton et al., 2020; Foley et al., 2008; Brent et al., 2015) or increasing opportunities for the social learning of complex feeding techniques (Lonsdorf et al., 2004; Estienne et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Samuni et al., 2020.

claim: Maternal presence can provide access to valuable ecological knowledge.
source: Maternal presence can also influence nutrition at these later stages of development by buffering against feeding competition (Samuni et al., 2020), providing access to valuable ecological knowledge (Stanton et al., 2020; Foley et al., 2008; Brent et al., 2015) or increasing opportunities for the social learning of complex feeding techniques (Lonsdorf et al., 2004; Estienne et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Stanton et al., 2020; Foley et al., 2008; Brent et al., 2015.

claim: Maternal presence can increase opportunities for the social learning of complex feeding techniques.
source: Maternal presence can also influence nutrition at these later stages of development by buffering against feeding competition (Samuni et al., 2020), providing access to valuable ecological knowledge (Stanton et al., 2020; Foley et al., 2008; Brent et al., 2015) or increasing opportunities for the social learning of complex feeding techniques (Lonsdorf et al., 2004; Estienne et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lonsdorf et al., 2004; Estienne et al., 2019.

claim: In social mammals, maternal loss can reduce offspring fitness across a broad age range through long-term effects on their social environment.
source: In social mammals maternal loss can therefore reduce the fitness of offspring across a broad age range through long-term effects on their social environment, negatively influencing their social integration and social status throughout their lives (Snyder-Mackler et al., 2020; Strauss et al., 2020; Tung et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on social mammals.

claim: Multiple studies have confirmed effects on survival for individuals orphaned well past the period of nutritional dependency.
source: Multiple studies have now confirmed effects on survival for individuals orphaned well past the period of nutritional dependency, with these negative changes to their social environment, often termed social adversity, posited to be the key mechanism by which this occurs (Andres et al., 2013; Stanton et al., 2020; Tung et al., 2016; Watts et al., 2009; Foster et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Social adversity is posited to be the key mechanism by which maternal loss reduces survival in social mammals.
source: Multiple studies have now confirmed effects on survival for individuals orphaned well past the period of nutritional dependency, with these negative changes to their social environment, often termed social adversity, posited to be the key mechanism by which this occurs (Andres et al., 2013; Stanton et al., 2020; Tung et al., 2016; Watts et al., 2009; Foster et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents a theoretical framework from the literature.

claim: In social mammals, the social environment can have extreme consequences for health, fitness, and lifespan.
source: In social mammals, the social environment can have extreme consequences for health, fitness, and lifespan, mediated through pathways such as chronic stress, immune function, or environmental exposure (Snyder-Mackler et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Snyder-Mackler et al., 2020.

claim: The impact of maternal loss varies based on the loss in benefits relative to individuals with mothers present.
source: The impact of maternal loss varies based on the loss in benefits relative to individuals with mothers present.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the discussion of differential effects across species and sexes.

claim: In species with sex-biased dispersal, the consequences of maternal loss can differ between the sexes.
source: In species with sex-biased dispersal, the consequences of maternal loss can differ between the sexes due to longer periods for potential investment in non-dispersing offspring (Clutton-Brock, 1991; Fairbanks, 2009; Altmann and Alberts, 2005; Greenwood, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on sex-biased dispersal and maternal investment.

claim: In female-philopatric red deer, maternal loss increases mortality for males and females.
source: In female-philopatric red deer (Cervus elaphus), maternal loss increases mortality for males and females, but this effect is only detectable in males under 2 years of age, whilst for females, maternal benefits continue throughout their lives (Andres et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Andres et al., 2013.

claim: In red deer, the effect of maternal loss on mortality is only detectable in males under 2 years of age.
source: In female-philopatric red deer (Cervus elaphus), maternal loss increases mortality for males and females, but this effect is only detectable in males under 2 years of age, whilst for females, maternal benefits continue throughout their lives (Andres et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Andres et al., 2013.

claim: In red deer, maternal benefits for females continue throughout their lives.
source: In female-philopatric red deer (Cervus elaphus), maternal loss increases mortality for males and females, but this effect is only detectable in males under 2 years of age, whilst for females, maternal benefits continue throughout their lives (Andres et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Andres et al., 2013.

claim: In male-philopatric chimpanzees, males that suffer maternal loss before reaching 15 years of age have lower survival.
source: In male-philopatric chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes), males that suffer maternal loss before reaching 15 years of age have lower survival, whilst females only show reduced survival from maternal loss under the age of 10 (Nakamura et al., 2014; Stanton et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nakamura et al., 2014 and Stanton et al., 2020.

claim: In chimpanzees, females only show reduced survival from maternal loss under the age of 10.
source: In male-philopatric chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes), males that suffer maternal loss before reaching 15 years of age have lower survival, whilst females only show reduced survival from maternal loss under the age of 10 (Nakamura et al., 2014; Stanton et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nakamura et al., 2014 and Stanton et al., 2020.

claim: In killer whales, maternal loss when offspring are over 30 years old reduces survival for both sexes, although considerably more so for males.
source: In killer whales (Orcinus orca), where neither sex disperses, maternal loss when offspring are over 30 years old reduces survival for both sexes, although considerably more so for males (Foster et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Foster et al., 2012.

claim: In killer whales, maternal loss between 15 and 30 years appears to reduce male but not female survival.
source: However, maternal loss between 15 and 30 years appears to reduce male but not female survival.
evidence: This is inferred from the discussion of killer whale maternal loss patterns in the context of Foster et al., 2012.

claim: Higher maternal investment in male killer whales is thought to be due to males mating outside the group and their offspring not increasing within-group feeding competition.
source: This is thought to be due to higher maternal investment in males which mate outside the group and whose offspring therefore do not increase within-group feeding competition.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed pattern in killer whales.

claim: Maternal loss not only influences offspring survival but can also impact other components of their offspring's fitness, such as reproduction and the survival of grand-offspring.
source: As a result of the numerous benefits mothers can provide, it is not surprising that maternal loss not only influences offspring survival but can also impact other components of their offspring's fitness, such as reproduction and the survival of grand-offspring.
evidence: This is supported by the examples provided in the subsequent sentences with citations.

claim: Male bonobos residing in groups with their mothers sire three times the number of offspring.
source: Male bonobos (Pan paniscus) residing in groups with their mothers sire three times the number of offspring (Surbeck et al., 2019), whilst maternal loss before weaning negatively affects antler development in male red deer – a trait found to correlate with reproductive success (Andres et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Surbeck et al., 2019.

claim: Maternal loss before weaning negatively affects antler development in male red deer.
source: Male bonobos (Pan paniscus) residing in groups with their mothers sire three times the number of offspring (Surbeck et al., 2019), whilst maternal loss before weaning negatively affects antler development in male red deer – a trait found to correlate with reproductive success (Andres et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Andres et al., 2013.

claim: Antler development in male red deer correlates with reproductive success.
source: Male bonobos (Pan paniscus) residing in groups with their mothers sire three times the number of offspring (Surbeck et al., 2019), whilst maternal loss before weaning negatively affects antler development in male red deer – a trait found to correlate with reproductive success (Andres et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Andres et al., 2013.

claim: In chimpanzees, females mature faster if their mothers are present.
source: In chimpanzees, females mature faster, first give birth younger (Walker et al., 2018) and enter the dominance hierarchy higher (Foerster et al., 2016) if their mothers are present which is expected to considerably increase their lifetime reproductive success.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walker et al., 2018.

claim: In chimpanzees, females first give birth younger if their mothers are present.
source: In chimpanzees, females mature faster, first give birth younger (Walker et al., 2018) and enter the dominance hierarchy higher (Foerster et al., 2016) if their mothers are present which is expected to considerably increase their lifetime reproductive success.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walker et al., 2018.

claim: In chimpanzees, females enter the dominance hierarchy higher if their mothers are present.
source: In chimpanzees, females mature faster, first give birth younger (Walker et al., 2018) and enter the dominance hierarchy higher (Foerster et al., 2016) if their mothers are present which is expected to considerably increase their lifetime reproductive success.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Foerster et al., 2016.

claim: Maternal presence in chimpanzees is expected to considerably increase female lifetime reproductive success.
source: In chimpanzees, females mature faster, first give birth younger (Walker et al., 2018) and enter the dominance hierarchy higher (Foerster et al., 2016) if their mothers are present which is expected to considerably increase their lifetime reproductive success.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited effects on maturation, age at first birth, and dominance.

claim: In savannah baboons, if mothers had themselves suffered maternal loss in the first 4 years of their life, their offspring had 48% higher mortality throughout the first 4 years of their life.
source: In savannah baboons (Papio cynocephalus), if mothers had themselves suffered maternal loss in the first 4 years of their life, their offspring had 48% higher mortality throughout the first 4 years of their life, suggesting an intergenerational effect of maternal loss driven by lifelong developmental constraints (Zipple et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zipple et al., 2019.

claim: The intergenerational effect of maternal loss in savannah baboons is driven by lifelong developmental constraints.
source: In savannah baboons (Papio cynocephalus), if mothers had themselves suffered maternal loss in the first 4 years of their life, their offspring had 48% higher mortality throughout the first 4 years of their life, suggesting an intergenerational effect of maternal loss driven by lifelong developmental constraints (Zipple et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a suggested mechanism from Zipple et al., 2019.

claim: Maternal loss in social mammals with extended maternal care can have long-term fitness consequences mediated through multiple pathways that detrimentally affect survival and reproduction.
source: Maternal loss in social mammals with extended maternal care can therefore have long-term fitness consequences mediated through multiple pathways that detrimentally affect survival and reproduction.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the multiple examples and citations provided in the preceding paragraphs.

claim: Highly social species often have the most to lose from maternal loss due to extended periods of mother–offspring co-residence and important social support mothers can provide.
source: Due to the extended periods of mother–offspring co-residence and the important social support mothers can provide, highly social species often have the most to lose from maternal loss.
evidence: This is an inference based on the established importance of maternal support in social species.

claim: Social groups provide the potential for support from other group members following maternal loss.
source: However, social groups also provide the potential for support from other group members following maternal loss.
evidence: This is supported by the examples and citations that follow.

claim: Both kin and non-kin group members have been suggested to compensate for the loss of close kin to varying extents.
source: Both kin and non-kin group members have been suggested to compensate for the loss of close kin to varying extents (Hamilton et al., 1982; Engh et al., 2006; Goldenberg and Wittemyer, 2017; Reddy and Mitani, 2019) and the strengthening of relationships with remaining group members may buffer against changing social environments (Firth et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The strengthening of relationships with remaining group members may buffer against changing social environments.
source: Both kin and non-kin group members have been suggested to compensate for the loss of close kin to varying extents (Hamilton et al., 1982; Engh et al., 2006; Goldenberg and Wittemyer, 2017; Reddy and Mitani, 2019) and the strengthening of relationships with remaining group members may buffer against changing social environments (Firth et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Firth et al., 2017.

claim: In chacma baboons, social support from group members is thought to alleviate the stress of losing a close relative.
source: In chacma baboons (Papio ursinus), social support from group members is thought to alleviate the stress of losing a close relative (Engh et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Engh et al., 2006.

claim: African savannah elephants associate more with group members of a similar age and siblings in response to maternal loss.
source: Similar social support has been suggested in African savannah elephants (Loxodonta africana) which associate more with group members of a similar age and siblings in response to maternal loss (Goldenberg and Wittemyer, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Goldenberg and Wittemyer, 2017.

claim: Orphaned elephants interact less with matriarchs which may decrease their access to key knowledge and high-quality resource patches.
source: However, these orphaned elephants interact less with matriarchs which may decrease their access to key knowledge and high-quality resource patches.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Goldenberg and Wittemyer, 2017 and represents a speculative mechanism.

claim: In chimpanzees, older siblings can 'adopt' younger siblings after maternal loss, increasing their social contact and showing heightened vigilance in dangerous situations.
source: In chimpanzees, older siblings can 'adopt' younger siblings after maternal loss, increasing their social contact and showing heightened vigilance in dangerous situations (Reddy and Mitani, 2019; Hobaiter et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Reddy and Mitani, 2019 and Hobaiter et al., 2014.

claim: Despite compensatory social behaviours, the negative consequences of maternal loss post-weaning are well documented in chimpanzees, baboons, and elephants.
source: But despite these compensatory social behaviours, the negative consequences of maternal loss post-weaning are well documented in all three genera (Stanton et al., 2020; Tung et al., 2016; Samuni et al., 2020; Nakamura et al., 2014; Goldenberg and Wittemyer, 2017; Goldenberg and Wittemyer, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on these species.

claim: Humans are a rare example of a group-living mammal in which compensatory social behaviours have been suggested to have the capacity to consistently overcome negative consequences of maternal loss.
source: Humans (Homo sapiens) are a rare example of a group-living mammal in which compensatory social behaviours have been suggested to have the capacity to consistently overcome these negative consequences of maternal loss.
evidence: This is supported by the meta-analysis results discussed in the following sentences.

claim: In a meta-analysis of historic and contemporary human populations, the death of a mother was associated with increased child mortality in all 28 populations studied.
source: In a meta-analysis of historic and contemporary human populations, the death of a mother was associated with increased child mortality in all 28 populations studied (Sear and Mace, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sear and Mace, 2008.

claim: The effect of maternal death on child mortality appeared to decline substantially with age in human populations.
source: However, this effect appeared to decline substantially with age, disappearing for children that suffered maternal loss over 2 years of age in 5 of the 11 populations in which it was investigated (Sear and Mace, 2008).

claim: The effect of maternal death disappeared for children that suffered maternal loss over 2 years of age in 5 of 11 human populations investigated.

evidence: This is supported by citation to Sear and Mace, 2008.

source: This reduced mortality was thought to be due to the care provided by other kin, particularly after weaning, suggesting that social buffering from other group members can overcome the negative effect of maternal loss on survival in certain circumstances.

claim: Social buffering from other group members can overcome the negative effect of maternal loss on survival in certain circumstances.
source: This reduced mortality was thought to be due to the care provided by other kin, particularly after weaning, suggesting that social buffering from other group members can overcome the negative effect of maternal loss on survival in certain circumstances.
evidence: This is an inference based on the human population data from Sear and Mace, 2008.

claim: There is evidence for the importance of fathers in child survival in human populations.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Hurtado and Hill, 1992 and Hill and Hurtado, 2017.

claim: In killer whales, maternal grandmothers, especially those that are post-reproductive, are known to improve grand-offspring survival.
source: In killer whales, maternal grandmothers, especially those that are post-reproductive, are also known to improve grand-offspring survival (Nattrass et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nattrass et al., 2019.

claim: Killer whales may represent a species in which care from other kin has the capacity to overcome the effects of maternal loss.
source: Whilst the specific effect of killer whale grandmothers on orphan survival has not been investigated, this finding suggests that killer whales may represent a further species in which care from other kin has the capacity to overcome the effects of maternal loss.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the grandmother effects observed.

claim: In humans, there is evidence for the benefits of care provided by non-kin such as step-mothers.
source: In humans, there is also evidence for the benefits of care provided by non-kin such as step-mothers (Andersson et al., 1996; Campbell and Lee, 2002) and through the modern practices of non-kin adoption (Bentley and Mace, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Andersson et al., 1996 and Campbell and Lee, 2002.

claim: In humans, there is evidence for the benefits of care through non-kin adoption.
source: In humans, there is also evidence for the benefits of care provided by non-kin such as step-mothers (Andersson et al., 1996; Campbell and Lee, 2002) and through the modern practices of non-kin adoption (Bentley and Mace, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bentley and Mace, 2009.

claim: Mountain gorillas show extended maternal care with offspring remaining in their natal groups at least until sexual maturity.
source: Mountain gorillas (Gorilla beringei beringei) show extended maternal care with offspring remaining in their natal groups at least until sexual maturity and approximately half remaining beyond sexual maturity (48% of females [Robbins et al., 2009a] and 55% of males [Stoinski et al., 2009a]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Robbins et al., 2009a and Stoinski et al., 2009a.

claim: Approximately 48% of female mountain gorillas remain in their natal groups beyond sexual maturity.
source: Mountain gorillas (Gorilla beringei beringei) show extended maternal care with offspring remaining in their natal groups at least until sexual maturity and approximately half remaining beyond sexual maturity (48% of females [Robbins et al., 2009a] and 55% of males [Stoinski et al., 2009a]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Robbins et al., 2009a.

claim: Approximately 55% of male mountain gorillas remain in their natal groups beyond sexual maturity.
source: Mountain gorillas (Gorilla beringei beringei) show extended maternal care with offspring remaining in their natal groups at least until sexual maturity and approximately half remaining beyond sexual maturity (48% of females [Robbins et al., 2009a] and 55% of males [Stoinski et al., 2009a]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stoinski et al., 2009a.

claim: Male mountain gorillas that disperse from their natal group tend to do so at a mean age of 15.3 years.
source: Females that disperse from their natal group tend to do so earlier (mean age of 7.9 years [Robbins et al., 2009a]) than males (mean age of 15.3 years [Stoinski et al., 2009a]) and therefore have a shorter period of potential maternal investment.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stoinski et al., 2009a.

claim: Female mountain gorillas have a shorter period of potential maternal investment than males due to earlier dispersal.
source: Females that disperse from their natal group tend to do so earlier (mean age of 7.9 years [Robbins et al., 2009a]) than males (mean age of 15.3 years [Stoinski et al., 2009a]) and therefore have a shorter period of potential maternal investment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the difference in dispersal ages.

claim: The complexity of gorilla social structure suggests that detrimental long-term effects on individual gorillas' social environments could have particularly negative fitness consequences.

claim: Approximately 36% of mountain gorilla groups contain multiple adult males.
source: Mountain gorilla groups either contain a single adult male (approximately 64% of groups) or multiple adult males (approximately 36% of groups) (Gray, 2010), at least one adult female, and their offspring (Robbins, 1995).

claim: Mountain gorilla infants are reliant on their mothers for thermoregulation and transport, being carried for prolonged periods.
source: Infants (<4 years of age) are nutritionally dependent on their mothers until being weaned at a mean of 3.3 years (Eckardt et al., 2016) and are reliant on their mothers for thermoregulation and transport, being carried for prolonged periods (Breuer et al., 2009).

evidence: This is a summary inference from the study findings.

claim: In mountain gorillas, like humans, social support appears to come from a number of group or family members.
source: In mountain gorillas, like humans (Sear and Mace, 2008; Lahdenperä et al., 2004; Sear et al., 2000; Hurtado and Hill, 1992; Andersson et al., 1996; Campbell and Lee, 2002; Bentley and Mace, 2009) social support appears to come from a number of group or family members.
evidence: This is a comparison supported by the data and citations to human studies.

claim: Social support from multiple group members could provide a buffer to the loss of any single relationship, even one as important as the mother–offspring relationship, once an individual can be nutritionally independent.
source: This could provide a buffer to the loss of any single relationship, even one as important as the mother–offspring relationship, once an individual can be nutritionally independent.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the mechanism of social buffering.

claim: In the absence of nepotistic matriarchal dominance hierarchies and when social buffering is possible due to cohesive strongly bonded social groups, it may matter less who is providing care as long as care is provided.
source: In the absence of nepotistic matriarchal dominance hierarchies and when social buffering is possible due to cohesive strongly bonded social groups, it may matter less who is providing care as long as care is provided.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about the conditions under which social buffering can overcome maternal loss.

claim: Mountain gorillas in the Volcanoes National Park, Rwanda, have been monitored almost continuously by the Dian Fossey Gorilla Fund's Karisoke Research Center since 1967.
source: Mountain gorillas in the Volcanoes National Park, Rwanda, have been monitored almost continuously by the Dian Fossey Gorilla Fund's Karisoke Research Center since 1967.

claim: Habituated mountain gorilla groups are monitored daily by field teams who collect data on demography, behaviour, ranging, and health.
source: Habituated mountain gorilla groups are monitored daily by field teams who collect data on demography, behaviour, ranging, and health.

claim: From 1967 to 2015 (inclusive), 59 (28 males, 31 females) out of the total 200 immature mountain gorillas (102 males, 98 females) that reached the age of at least 2 years suffered maternal loss between the ages of 2 and 8.
source: From 1967 to 2015 (inclusive), 59 (28 males, 31 females) out of the total 200 immature mountain gorillas (102 males, 98 females) that reached the age of at least 2 years suffered maternal loss between the ages of 2 and 8 through the death or permanent transfer of their mother.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic about the study sample.

claim: The youngest infant to survive maternal loss was a 2.45-year-old female.
source: The youngest infant to survive maternal loss was a 2.45-year-old female.

source: Three infants aged 1.91, 2.42, and 2.52 became separated from their mothers after a suspected poacher encounter.

source: The 2.42-year-old died after 9 days of separation.

claim: Focal data collected daily in each group were used to construct social networks based on 2 m proximity and affiliative contact.
source: Focal data collected daily in each group were used to construct social networks based on (a) 2 m proximity and (b) affiliative contact (resting, playing, or feeding in physical contact and grooming, but excluding physical aggression) for the 6 months leading up to a maternal loss incident and the 6 months immediately after a maternal loss incident.
evidence: This describes the methods for social network construction.

claim: Habituated gorilla groups were monitored for up to 4 hrs daily and all gorillas were individually identified by physical characteristics.
source: Habituated gorilla groups were monitored for up to 4 hrs daily and all gorillas were individually identified by physical characteristics.
evidence: This describes the data collection protocol.

claim: Behavioural data were collected on each group member via 50 min focal sampling during which the researcher would typically be within 10–20 m of the focal individual.
source: Behavioural data were collected on each group member via 50 min focal sampling during which the researcher would typically be within 10–20 m of the focal individual.
evidence: This describes the data collection protocol.

claim: During focal sampling, a focal scan was completed every 10 min which recorded all gorillas within 2 m of the focal individual and all gorillas in physical contact with the focal individual.
source: During focal sampling, a focal scan was completed every 10 min which recorded all gorillas within 2 m of the focal individual and all gorillas in physical contact with the focal individual.

claim: The focal sampling approach limited the extent of potential sampling bias due to individual-level differences in observation propensity.
source: This focal sampling approach limited the extent of potential sampling bias due to individual-level differences in observation propensity, with all group members systematically observed and an extremely low likelihood of individuals within 2 m or in physical contact of the focal individual being missed at these close proximities.
